posts.title: Context windows changed agent architecture
posts.hook:
I stopped building multi-agent orchestration last month.

Not because it doesn't work. Because a single agent with a 1M token context window does 80% of what my four-agent pipeline did.
posts.body:
I stopped building multi-agent orchestration last month.

Not because it doesn't work. Because a single agent with a 1M token context window does 80% of what my four-agent pipeline did.

The old pattern: split tasks across specialized agents, pass context through handoff docs, pray nothing got lost in translation. I had a router agent, a research agent, a writer agent, and a QA agent. Four system prompts. Four failure points. One fragile chain.

Now I load the entire codebase into one session. Voice DNA files, anti-slop rules, project context, relevant data... all in one window. The agent holds the full picture.

What actually changed:

✅ No more context handoff bugs between agents
✅ No more "the research agent found X but the writer agent forgot it"
✅ Debugging went from "which agent dropped the ball" to reading one conversation

The tradeoff is real though. Costs went up ~40% per session. Token usage is brutal when you're loading 200k+ of context every run. And latency on that first response is noticeable.

But the reliability improvement is worth it. I went from ~60% first-attempt success rate on complex content tasks to ~85%.

The architecture lesson: don't distribute complexity until a single node actually can't handle it. We were building microservices when a monolith worked fine.
posts.cta: Anyone else consolidating their agent pipelines back down? Curious what broke when you tried.

remixes.label: complexity-hangover
remixes.hook: My four-agent pipeline was an engineering flex, not a product decision.
remixes.body:
My four-agent pipeline was an engineering flex, not a product decision.

I built it because distributed systems are interesting. A router that parsed intent. A researcher that pulled sources. A writer that drafted. A QA bot that checked tone and facts. Clean architecture. Good separation of concerns.

Also: four points of failure, context bleeding between handoffs, and a debugging experience that made me mass print JSON diffs at 11pm.

Then Claude's context window hit 1M tokens. I loaded the same system prompt, reference docs, voice files, and task description into one session. No orchestration. No handoff protocol. No "lost in translation" bugs.

It handled maybe 80% of what the pipeline did. The 20% it missed? Edge cases I'd over-engineered solutions for that barely mattered.

The lesson wasn't "multi-agent is dead." It's that most multi-agent setups exist because we built around a constraint that just evaporated. When context windows were 8K, splitting work across agents was necessary. At 1M, it's often just added complexity.

Before you architect a multi-agent system, ask: am I solving a real coordination problem, or am I working around a context limit that no longer exists?

remixes.body:
Here's the exact moment I knew my multi-agent system was over-engineered.

Agent 3 asked Agent 1 for context that was already in the original prompt.

I had four agents. Router parsed the task. Researcher gathered references. Writer drafted. QA checked. Clean on a whiteboard. Messy in production.

The failure mode wasn't any single agent. It was the space between them. Context handoff docs that drifted from reality. A QA agent that flagged tone issues because it didn't have the voice examples the writer used. A router that misclassified tasks 15% of the time.

I ran an experiment. Took one content task. Loaded everything into a single 1M context session: system prompt, 12 voice DNA files, 40 example posts, the task brief, relevant source material. Total: about 180K tokens.

Result: same quality output in one pass. No handoffs. No serialization bugs. No orchestration code to maintain.

I kept multi-agent for one thing: parallel execution where tasks are genuinely independent. Research three companies simultaneously, then merge. That's real parallelism. Everything else collapsed into single-context.

The rule I use now: if agents need to share context to do their jobs, they probably shouldn't be separate agents.

posts.title: Memory is the moat for production agents
posts.hook:
The teams shipping real AI agents aren't the ones fine-tuning models.

They're the ones who figured out memory.
posts.body:
The teams shipping real AI agents aren't the ones fine-tuning models.

They're the ones who figured out memory.

I run a content pipeline where Claude writes LinkedIn posts, blog drafts, and Reddit comments in my voice. The model is the same one everyone else has access to. The difference is ~18 months of accumulated voice DNA, anti-slop patterns, and lessons learned sitting in markdown files that load into every session.

That's memory. Not RAG over a vector database. Not fine-tuning. Flat files with hard-won rules like "never use em-dashes" and "don't open with origin story unless the piece is explicitly about origin story."

The pattern I keep seeing in production agent systems:

1. Start with a good prompt
2. Ship it, watch it fail in specific ways
3. Write a rule for each failure
4. Load those rules into every future session
5. Repeat for months

After enough cycles, your agent isn't generic anymore. It's yours. And that compound knowledge is genuinely hard to replicate because it came from real failure modes, not hypothetical ones.

The model is commodity. The memory is the asset.

This is why I keep everything in version-controlled markdown instead of a proprietary platform. If the model changes, the memory transfers. If the platform dies, the memory survives.

remixes.body:
Fine-tuning is the wrong answer for 90% of production agent use cases.

Memory files are cheaper, faster to iterate, and you can actually read them.

I've been running a content agent for 18 months. It writes in my voice across four platforms. The voice quality has gone from "obviously AI" to "people can't tell" over that time. I never fine-tuned anything.

Here's what I did instead: built a memory layer out of markdown files. Voice principles that describe how I write. Anti-patterns that list specific phrases to never use. A lessons file that gets a new entry every time I correct the agent. Example posts tagged by quality and platform.

When the agent runs, these files load into context. The model reads my accumulated preferences, patterns, and corrections before it writes a single word.

Why this beats fine-tuning for my use case:

1. I can edit a markdown file and see the change immediately. No training run. No waiting.
2. I can read every instruction the agent follows. Total transparency.
3. When the base model improves, my memory layer automatically benefits. Fine-tuned models are frozen at training time.
4. Cost is zero beyond the context tokens. No training compute.

Fine-tuning has its place. But if your first instinct for customization is "let's fine-tune," you're probably skipping the simpler solution that works for most cases.

posts.title: Coding agents amplify seniority
posts.hook:
Claude Code doesn't mass-produce junior engineers.

It gives senior engineers mass production capability.
posts.body:
Claude Code doesn't mass-produce junior engineers.

It gives senior engineers mass production capability.

I shipped a full content distribution pipeline last month. Discord webhooks, CLI approval flow, blog publishing, multi-platform formatting. Maybe 3,000 lines of Python across a dozen files. Took about a week of evening sessions.

Without Claude Code, that's a 3-4 week project minimum. With it, the bottleneck shifted entirely from "can I write this code" to "do I know what to build."

That's the part people miss. The agent can write the code. It can't decide the architecture. It can't smell a bad abstraction forming. It can't say "this approach will break when we add a second content type" unless you already know to ask.

Every time I give it a vague instruction, I get vague output. Every time I give it a precise spec with clear constraints, I get production-quality code on the first pass.

The precision of the input determines the quality of the output. And precision comes from experience.

So the gap between a senior engineer with Claude Code and a junior engineer with Claude Code isn't shrinking. It's widening. The senior ships 10x more because they know what to specify. The junior ships faster too, but they're still learning what to build.
posts.cta: The real skill now isn't writing code. It's writing specs. How are you adapting?

The staff engineer wrote: "Build a CLI in Python using Click. Input: CSV with columns company_name, domain, employee_count. For each row, call the Clearbit API to get industry and funding. Score using: 50+ employees = 2 points, SaaS industry = 3 points, Series A+ = 2 points. Output: sorted CSV with score column, descending. Handle API rate limits with exponential backoff. Skip rows where domain is empty."

Same model. Same tool. Wildly different output.

The staff engineer didn't write better prompts. They wrote a better spec. They knew what edge cases to anticipate, what architecture decisions to make upfront, and what "done" looks like.

Claude Code amplifies whatever engineering judgment you bring to it. If you bring vague requirements, you get vague code. If you bring precise specs, you get working software.

This is why the "AI will replace developers" framing is backwards. AI replaces the typing. The thinking got more valuable.

posts.hook:

posts.body:
Two years ago I called myself a "GTM engineer" and people asked if I meant sales ops.

Now there are job postings for it.

The role sits at the intersection of ops, data, and building. You're not managing Salesforce fields. You're writing Python scripts that pull intent signals from Reddit, enrich them through waterfall APIs, score them in SQLite, and push qualified leads into sequences.

The spray-and-pray SDR needed volume because the targeting was bad. Better targeting means you need fewer sends. Fewer sends means each one matters more. Each one mattering more means you need someone who can build the system that finds the right person at the right time.

That's not an SDR. That's not a rev ops person. That's an engineer who understands go-to-market.

What I'm seeing in practice: one GTM engineer with coding agents replaces the output of a 3-person SDR team. Not because they work harder. Because the system they build runs 24/7 and doesn't send garbage.

The uncomfortable part for sales leaders: this means smaller teams with higher individual output. The 50-seat SDR floor is becoming a 5-person technical team with better results.

If you're in sales ops right now and you're not learning to code (or learning to use coding agents), the window is closing fast.

Monday: built a signal monitor that watches competitor job postings for patterns that indicate they're losing customers.

Tuesday: wrote an enrichment waterfall. Lead comes in, hits Clearbit first. If Clearbit misses, falls through to Apollo. Then PDL. Three providers, one clean record.

Wednesday: debugging why the scoring model weighted employee count too heavily. Adjusted the coefficients. Re-ran against last quarter's closed-won to validate.

Thursday: shipped a Slack bot that pings the sales team when a scored lead crosses the threshold.

None of this lives in a platform. It's Python scripts, SQLite databases, cron jobs, and API calls. Duct tape that works better than the $50K tools it replaced.

The role exists because modern GTM has a building problem, not a buying problem.

posts.title: First-party signals vs bought lists
posts.hook:
Same campaign. Same copy. Same sender.

One list bought from a data vendor. One list built from first-party signals.

Reply rate: 2.1% vs 9.4%.
posts.body:
Same campaign. Same copy. Same sender.

One list bought from a data vendor. One list built from first-party signals.

Reply rate: 2.1% vs 9.4%.

The first-party list was smaller. 340 contacts vs 2,200. Built from job postings (hiring for roles our tool replaces), Reddit threads (asking about problems we solve), and tech stack changes (removing a competitor from their site).

The vendor list was "ICP matched." Right industry, right company size, right title. All the firmographic boxes checked. But no timing signal. No evidence they care about this problem right now.

Timing beats targeting every time.

Building first-party signal lists takes more work upfront. I run a daily scrape across Reddit, job boards, and BuiltWith. The script enriches matches through Apollo, scores them, and drops qualified leads into a review queue. Maybe 30 minutes of setup, then it runs on its own.

The economics are backwards from what most teams expect. The "cheap" vendor list costs $0.15/contact but converts at 2%. The "expensive" first-party list costs maybe $0.80/contact in API calls but converts at 9%.

Cost per meeting: $7.50 on first-party signals vs $15+ on the vendor list.

Stop buying lists. Build signal pipelines.

Your 2,000-contact list is losing to someone's 300-contact list.

Here's how a smaller list wins. Every contact on it did something publicly that signals they need what you sell. Not "fits your ICP." Not "matches firmographic criteria." Actually demonstrated a need.

Three signals I build lists from:

1. Job postings for roles our product replaces. If they're hiring a full-time person to do what our tool automates, that's a buying signal, not a firmographic match.

2. Reddit and community threads asking about the exact problem we solve. These people are actively looking. They told the internet they have a pain point.

3. Tech stack removals. When a company drops a competitor from their site, they're either consolidating or shopping. Either way, they're in motion.

The contact count is smaller because real signals are rare. Most companies aren't actively doing any of these things at any given time. But the ones who are? They reply at 4x the rate of a bought list.

Volume-based outbound trains you to accept bad reply rates and compensate with scale. Signal-based outbound trains you to find the 340 people who actually want to hear from you.

posts.title: 6 micro-SaaS in 90 days reality check
posts.hook: Shipping 6 products in 90 days sounds impressive until you ask which ones have paying users.
posts.body:
Shipping 6 products in 90 days sounds impressive until you ask which ones have paying users.

I've been building with AI coding tools for over a year. Shipped dozens of internal tools, a few public ones. The speed is real. You can absolutely go from idea to deployed product in a weekend.

But speed of building and speed of finding product-market fit are completely different things.

I built a Reddit scraping tool in two days. Took another two months to figure out that the real product wasn't the scraper, it was the intent scoring layer on top of it. The coding agent built both versions fast. Neither version mattered until I understood what customers actually wanted.

The pattern I see with rapid-shipping builders:

- Ship fast, learn what doesn't work
- Ship fast again, learn what almost works
- Slow down on the third thing because now you have real users giving real feedback
- That third thing becomes the actual business

The first two weren't wasted. They were research disguised as products.

The trap is staying in shipping mode forever. Always launching, never iterating. AI tools make launching so easy that iteration feels boring by comparison. But iteration is where the money is.

One product with 50 paying users teaches you more than six products with zero.

posts.body:
I run ~15 AI agent tasks daily. Content generation, lead scoring, Reddit scraping, CRM updates, voice drift checks.

Monthly cost: roughly $400 in API tokens. That replaces about $8k/month in tooling and contractor work.

But the cost structure is nothing like traditional SaaS. It's spiky. One complex coding session can burn $30 in tokens. A simple cron job that scores 50 leads costs $0.40. There's no flat monthly fee, no predictable line item for the CFO.

What I've learned about managing agent costs:

✅ Batch similar tasks. Running 50 enrichments in one session is cheaper than 50 individual calls
✅ Use the right model for the job. Haiku for classification, Sonnet for drafting, Opus for architecture decisions
✅ Cache aggressively. Voice DNA files don't change daily, so I load them once and reference the cache
✅ Set token budgets per task type. Content drafts get 8k output max. Research gets 4k

The biggest cost driver isn't the obvious stuff. It's context loading. Every session that loads 150k tokens of project context before doing anything costs real money. I cut costs 30% by splitting my CLAUDE.md into conditional sections that only load when relevant.

The unit economics work. But you have to treat token spend like cloud infrastructure, not like a software subscription. Monitor it, optimize it, budget for spikes.

✅ Set token budgets per task type. Content drafts get 8k output max. Research gets 4k

The biggest cost driver isn't the obvious stuff. It's context loading. Every session that loads 150k tokens of project context before doing anything costs real money. I cut costs 30% by splitting my CLAUDE.md into conditional sections that only load when relevant.

The unit economics work. But you have to treat token spend like cloud infrastructure, not like a software subscription. Monitor it, optimize it, budget for spikes.

posts.body:
I was a plumber for ten years before I touched a CRM.

The best thing that background gave me wasn't grit. It was systems thinking.

Plumbing is literally building systems. Water comes in, gets distributed, waste goes out. Every joint matters. One bad connection upstream ruins everything downstream. You don't patch leaks with tape, you find the root cause and fix it properly.

GTM engineering is the same thing. Data comes in from signals. Gets enriched and scored through a pipeline. Qualified leads flow out to sequences. One bad enrichment step upstream (wrong email provider, stale data) ruins your deliverability downstream.

When I see someone closing their first B2B contract between school pickups, or shipping a product after leaving a nursing career, the pattern is always the same. They bring domain knowledge from their previous life that gives them an edge nobody else in the space has.

The nurse who built a patient scheduling tool understands workflow pain that a Stanford CS grad never will. The teacher who built an EdTech product knows what actually happens in a classroom.

Non-traditional backgrounds aren't a disadvantage to overcome. They're a moat. You see problems that pure-tech founders can't see because you lived inside those problems for years.

AI coding tools just removed the last barrier. You don't need to be a developer to build software anymore. You need to understand the problem deeply enough to specify the solution.

The best GTM engineer I know used to install HVAC systems.

That's not a motivational story. It's a competitive advantage.

Trades teach you something that computer science degrees don't: every system is physical before it's digital. Water pressure, airflow, electrical load. You learn that upstream decisions create downstream consequences. That shortcuts create debt. That the elegant solution is usually the one with fewer moving parts.

I spent a decade in plumbing before I ever logged into a CRM. The mental models transferred directly.

Diagnosing a slow pipeline is the same as diagnosing low water pressure. You start at the source and trace the flow. Is the problem at the top of funnel (supply), in the middle (blockage), or at the end (capacity)? You don't guess. You test each stage.

Building integrations between tools is plumbing, literally. Data flows from one system to another through connectors. Every junction is a potential leak. Every transform is a fitting that needs to be the right size.

The non-obvious trades advantage isn't "grit" or "work ethic." Every LinkedIn post about career pivots mentions those. The actual advantage is that you've spent years working in systems where the feedback is immediate and physical. A bad pipe joint leaks. Right now. On your shoes. There's no sprint retro. Just consequences.

That feedback loop trains a kind of precision that's rare in software.

remixes.body:
Career pivot content usually goes like this: "I left my boring job, followed my passion, and now I'm thriving."

Here's the version nobody posts.

I was a plumber for ten years. I didn't leave because I was bored or because I "found my calling." I left because the physical toll was unsustainable and I needed to build something that didn't depend on my body showing up every day.

The transition was not clean. I didn't go from wrench to keyboard in a montage. I spent two years doing both, learning CRM administration on nights and weekends while still running service calls during the day. The skills transfer was real but not instant.

What transferred: systems thinking. Plumbing is designing systems where water flows from source to destination without leaks, blockages, or pressure drops. GTM engineering is designing systems where leads flow from source to destination without data loss, bottlenecks, or attribution gaps. Same mental model, different medium.

What didn't transfer: the confidence to speak up in rooms full of people with CS degrees and startup pedigrees. That took years. I still catch myself adding caveats that software-native people never add.

The "non-obvious background advantage" framing is popular on LinkedIn. And it's partly true. But it skips the uncomfortable middle part where your background feels like a liability before it becomes an asset.

Ten years of plumbing made me a better GTM engineer. It also made me feel like an imposter for the first three.

Career transitions from trades into technology are more common than people think, and they come with a genuine structural advantage that gets underestimated.

I spent a decade in plumbing before moving into GTM engineering. The transferable skill wasn't discipline or work ethic, though those matter. It was systems thinking.

Plumbing is fundamentally about designing systems. Water enters, gets distributed to where it's needed, waste exits. Every joint, every fitting, every gradient matters. One bad connection upstream creates problems everywhere downstream. You learn to trace problems from source to symptom, not guess at random.

That mental model maps directly to GTM infrastructure. Data flows from lead sources through enrichment, scoring, routing, and into CRM. Every integration point is a potential leak. If you're coming from a trades or operational background into tech, I'd recommend two things. First, stop underselling your systems experience. It's rarer in tech than you think. Second, learn the vocabulary fast. The mental models are the same, but you need to speak the language to be taken seriously.

Your background isn't a gap in your resume. It's a lens that most of your peers simply don't have.

LinkedIn loves a career pivot story. "I used to be a plumber, now I'm a GTM engineer. Trades taught me grit."

That framing is lazy and it undersells the actual advantage.

Grit is not what trades teach you. Every job on earth requires grit. What trades actually teach you is systems thinking at a level that most software people never develop.

It leaks on your shoes right now. You learn to build things correctly the first time because the feedback loop is instant.

Software lets you be sloppy. Ship the bug, fix it later. Push the hack, refactor someday. In plumbing, there is no "fix it later." The building fails inspection. The customer has no water. Your work is tested in real time.

That training creates a precision that I see missing constantly in GTM. People build pipelines with leaky integrations, broken handoffs, and data flowing nowhere. Then they wonder why conversion rates are bad. They need a plumber.

The tech industry has a credentialism problem. CS degree, startup pedigree, "5+ years in SaaS." Meanwhile, the person who spent a decade building actual physical systems brings a mental model that's worth more than any bootcamp certificate.

The trades-to-tech pipeline isn't a feel-good story. It's an unfair advantage.
